source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: The Best Trades: Putting It All Together

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; sides field states mirrored/same

candidates.name: TrendBarBody
candidates.quote: the reversal signal bar should be strong
candidates.description: Classifies the current bar as a strong bull (or bear) trend bar: it closes near its high (low) and its body is most of its range. Used throughout this chapter as the signal-bar quality test for every setup listed below.

complexity.reason: single-bar arithmetic on OHLC

notes: Foundational primitive; every setup below that requires 'a strong signal bar' depends on this.

candidates.name: SignalBarDirectionRequirement
candidates.quote: Buy only above bull bars and short below bear bars.
candidates.description: A long entry is only valid if the signal bar (the bar the stop-entry price is measured from) itself closed as a bull bar; mirrored for shorts. This gates every stop-entry setup in the chapter.

complexity.reason: single prior-bar close/open comparison plus current-bar breakout

notes: Stated as its own guideline, separate from any specific pattern; used as a blanket filter on all stop entries.

candidates.name: PullbackLegCount
candidates.quote: look for high 2 and wedge... setups
candidates.description: Counts how many separate down-legs (for a bull pullback) or up-legs (for a bear pullback) have occurred since the most recent swing extreme, where a leg ends when price makes a new extreme beyond the prior pullback low/high. Returned as an integer used by the High-1/2 and Low-1/2 setups below.
candidates.pseudocode: int legs = countLegsSinceSwingExtreme(direction, lookback)  // helper: increments when a new local extreme against 'direction' forms, separated by at least one bar that closed back toward 'direction'

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection and leg segmentation over a variable-length window

notes: Brooks never gives a precise algorithm for 'a leg'; this is a design decision the authoring pass must make once and reuse.

candidates.name: PullbackEntryOneLeg
candidates.quote: Buying a high 1 pullback in a strong bull spike in a bull trend, but not after a strong buy climax.
candidates.description: In a bull trend, buy one tick above the high of the first pullback bar after a new swing high (a 'high 1'); mirrored: in a bear trend, sell one tick below the low of the first pullback bar after a new swing low ('low 1').
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.AlwaysInLong() && PullbackLegCount(down,lookback)==1 && TrendBarBody(bull) && close[0] < high[highestSince(1)] && high[1] > high[0]

complexity.reason: depends on leg counting (V24-03) and an always-in read

candidates.name: PullbackEntryTwoLeg
candidates.quote: Buying a high 2 pullback to the moving average in a bull trend.
candidates.description: In a bull trend, buy one tick above the high of the second down-leg pullback bar ('high 2'), especially when that bar touches or penetrates the 20-bar EMA; mirrored 'low 2' for bear trends.

complexity.reason: leg counting plus an EMA-touch test

candidates.name: TwoBarReversal
candidates.quote: Bar 7 was a two-bar reversal buy setup because it was a high 2 down from bar 6 and a double bottom bull flag with bar 5.
candidates.description: A two-bar reversal: bar[1] made a new extreme in the prevailing direction, and bar[0] closes strongly the opposite way with a range overlapping bar[1], forming a combined signal. Buy above the high of bar[0].
candidates.pseudocode: low[1] < lowest(low,swingLookback,2) && close[0] > open[0] && close[0] > close[1] && low[0] <= low[1]+overlapTicks*tickSize

complexity.reason: cross-bar comparison against a short local extreme, no full swing detection needed

candidates.name: DoubleTopBottom
candidates.quote: Bar 25 was a two-bar reversal, and it formed a double bottom with bar 23.
candidates.description: Price forms two swing lows (highs) within a lookback window at approximately the same level, with a bounce between them; the second touch is the signal for a reversal or fade.
candidates.pseudocode: double = abs(swingLow(0) - swingLow(1)) <= tolTicks*tickSize && barsBetween(swingLow(0),swingLow(1)) <= maxLegBars

complexity.reason: requires swing-pivot detection and comparing two pivots for level and spacing

candidates.name: WedgeFlagPullback
candidates.quote: Buying a wedge bull flag pullback in a bull trend.
candidates.description: A three-push pullback against the trend (wedge) where each push is a marginal new extreme with decreasing momentum; buy the failure of the third push. Mirrored for bear-trend wedge flags.
candidates.pseudocode: pushCount(direction,lookback)==3 && each push is a marginal new extreme (within tolerance) beyond the prior push && TrendBarBody(counterTrend) on the 3rd push

complexity.reason: requires pivot/push detection with a marginal-new-extreme test across three legs

candidates.name: FinalFlagReversal
candidates.quote: Strong final flag reversal after a swing up or down in a trading range or weak channel.
candidates.description: A small, tight consolidation (flag) that forms at the end of an extended trend leg or trading-range swing and then breaks in the opposite direction, signaling exhaustion of that leg.
candidates.pseudocode: isSmallFlag(lookback) && barsSinceLegStart(direction) >= minLegBars && TrendBarBody(oppositeOfLeg) && close[0] beyond flag boundary against 'direction'

complexity.reason: needs both a tight-consolidation test and identification of the preceding leg's length

candidates.name: BreakoutPullbackEntry
candidates.quote: Buying a breakout pullback after a breakout from a bull flag in a bull trend.
candidates.description: After a bull (bear) bar closes above (below) a prior flag/range, the very next pullback that holds is a buy (sell) setup one tick beyond that pullback bar.
candidates.pseudocode: brokeOutAbove = close[1] > highest(high,flagLookback,2) && TrendBarBody(bull)[1] && !brokeOutAboveFlaggedYet && close[0] < close[1]

complexity.reason: cross-bar state tracking a recent breakout plus one pullback bar

candidates.name: MovingAverageGapBar
candidates.quote: the bar 25 first moving average gap bar in the larger bull trend, which is often a buy signal
candidates.description: The first bar in a trend that gaps to the opposite side of the 20-bar EMA (e.g. the first bear-trend bar whose entire range is below the EMA) after a run of bars mostly on the trend side, signaling renewed momentum; entry is one tick beyond that bar in the trend direction.
candidates.pseudocode: allBarsAbove = high[1] > ema[1] // prior N bars mostly above ema; gapBar = high[0] < ema[0] && close[0] < open[0]

complexity.reason: EMA comparison plus a short run-state check on prior bars

candidates.name: AlwaysInDirection
candidates.quote: the market probably became always-in long as it traded above the strong bar 5 reversal bar
candidates.description: A persistent read of which side (long/short/flat) is currently in control based on the balance of trend bars, breakouts, and failures; used as a context gate for every with-trend entry in this chapter (e.g. 'once always-in long, buy pullbacks').
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.AlwaysInLong() // design-decision helper: some function of recent trend-bar count, breakout success, and swing structure

complexity.reason: Brooks defines this qualitatively as a discretionary read of overall control; a concrete bar-level algorithm needs a design decision before coding

notes: This is the single most load-bearing gate in the chapter; nearly every 'best trade' bullet is conditioned on an always-in read.

candidates.name: TrendLineBreak
candidates.quote: Following a strong break of the trend line, look for a weak trend resumption to fail on a test of the trend's extreme
candidates.description: Price closes beyond a trend line drawn across the most recent swing pivots in the trend direction, signaling the trend's momentum has broken.
candidates.pseudocode: trendLine = projectLine(pivots(direction,lookback)); broke = (direction==up ? close[0] < trendLine[0] : close[0] > trendLine[0])

complexity.reason: needs pivot detection and line projection from at least two pivots

candidates.name: MajorTrendReversalSetup
candidates.quote: Major trend reversal: Following a strong break of the trend line, look for a weak trend resumption to fail on a test of the trend's extreme; the reversal signal bar should be strong. After a bear trend, look to buy a higher low, double bottom, or lower low.
candidates.description: A major trend reversal: (1) a strong trend-line break with momentum, (2) a subsequent test of the trend's extreme that fails (higher low / double bottom / lower low after a downtrend; mirrored for an uptrend), (3) a strong reversal signal bar on that test.
candidates.pseudocode: TrendLineBreak(direction) && barsSince(TrendLineBreak) <= testWindow && priceTestsExtreme(direction, tolTicks) && TrendBarBody(oppositeOfDirection)

complexity.reason: composes a trend-line break, a swing-extreme test, and a signal-bar quality check

candidates.name: MeasuredMoveTarget
candidates.quote: Trading when the channel in a spike and channel day or the breakout in a trending trading range day reaches a measured move target and the move is weakening.
candidates.description: Project a profit target (or reversal expectation) equal to the height of the initial spike/leg, added to (subtracted from) the breakout point; treat arrival at that level plus a weakening signal bar as an exit or fade cue.
candidates.pseudocode: spikeHeight = highest(high,spikeLookback)-lowest(low,spikeLookback); target = breakoutPrice + spikeHeight; exitOrFade = close[0] >= target && TrendBarBody(opposite)

complexity.reason: a window high/low measurement projected forward from a known breakout price

candidates.name: StairsPatternReversal
candidates.quote: Buying a third or fourth push down in a bear stairs pattern for a test of the low of the prior push down.
candidates.description: In a 'stairs' trend (a series of small pushes each making a marginal new extreme with a brief pause between), fade the third or fourth consecutive push, targeting a test of the low (high) of the push before it. Mirrored for a bull stairs pattern.

complexity.reason: needs a push-counter over marginal new extremes, similar to wedge detection but without convergence

candidates.name: TradingRangeBoundaryFade
candidates.quote: Shorting at the top of a trading range, especially if it is a second entry. Buying at the bottom of a trading range, especially if it is a second entry.
candidates.description: Fade a touch of the top (bottom) of an established N-bar trading range: sell (buy) on a reversal signal bar there.
candidates.pseudocode: rangeHigh = highest(high,rangeLookback); rangeLow = lowest(low,rangeLookback); atTop = high[0] >= rangeHigh - tolTicks*tickSize; fade = atTop && TrendBarBody(bear)

complexity.reason: a highest/lowest window comparison plus a signal-bar test

candidates.name: SecondEntrySignal
candidates.quote: Shorting at the top of a trading range, especially if it is a second entry.
candidates.description: A first signal in a given direction fails (price does not follow through and returns to test the same level); the second occurrence of the same setup within a short window is taken with higher confidence.

complexity.reason: cross-bar state remembering that a prior instance of the same setup occurred and failed

candidates.name: ExpandingTriangleReversal
candidates.quote: Expanding triangle bottoms are always major trend reversal setups.
candidates.description: A reversal pattern of three (or more) swing pivots in the same direction where each new pivot is a larger extreme than the last (expanding, not converging like a wedge); the failure of the final, most extreme push is the entry.

complexity.reason: pivot detection with a strictly-increasing-amplitude test across three or more legs

candidates.name: ClimaxBar
candidates.quote: Whenever there is a trend of 10 or 20 or more bars and it then has a huge bull trend bar, the bar often represents exhaustion.
candidates.description: After an extended run in one direction, a single trend bar whose range is a large multiple of the recent average range signals likely exhaustion (a buy or sell climax) and increases the chance of at least a two-legged correction.

complexity.reason: an average-range window comparison plus a bar-count-since-trend-start state

candidates.name: MicroChannelBreakout
candidates.quote: If there is a bear micro channel down to the bottom of the range, wait for the bull breakout and look to buy the pullback
candidates.description: A micro channel is 4+ consecutive same-direction, heavily overlapping trend bars with no real pullback. Do not enter on its first breakout; wait for the breakout to hold and enter on the first pullback from it (a form of BreakoutPullbackEntry gated by a preceding micro-channel).
candidates.pseudocode: microChannelBars = countConsecutiveOverlappingTrendBars(direction) >= 4; brokeOut = microChannelBars[1] && close[0] closes beyond channel against direction; entry = brokeOut[1] && pullback[0]

complexity.reason: a consecutive-bar counter with an overlap test, then reuses the breakout-pullback primitive

candidates.name: MinRewardToRiskFilter
candidates.quote: Take a trade only where you are going for a reward that is at least as large as your risk.
candidates.description: Before entering, require that the planned profit target distance is at least a multiple of the planned protective-stop distance (the multiple is 1x for scalps, 2x for swings per the guidelines below).
candidates.pseudocode: plannedReward = abs(targetPrice - entryPrice); plannedRisk = abs(entryPrice - stopPrice); plannedReward >= minRewardMultiple*plannedRisk

complexity.reason: a comparison of two already-known price distances, no bar history needed

candidates.name: MaxTradesPerDaySwitch
candidates.quote: Look for only three to five reasonable trades a day. If in doubt, stay out.
candidates.description: Once the count of trades taken today reaches a cap, block further entries for the rest of the session.

complexity.reason: requires a persistent same-session trade counter reset at each new day

candidates.name: OpeningRangeSwingReversal
candidates.quote: Opening reversals where the setup is strong: Swing for a reward that is at least twice the risk: the probability of success is 50 to 60 percent.
candidates.description: During the opening range, a strong reversal signal (composes the general reversal/signal-bar primitives) taken with a swing profit target at least twice the planned risk.

complexity.reason: inherits the hard complexity of the reversal primitives it composes, gated to the opening bars

candidates.name: OpeningRangeScalpReversal
candidates.quote: Scalp for a reward that is at least as large as the risk: the probability is about 60 to 70 percent.
candidates.description: Same opening-range reversal setup as V24-24 but scalped with a 1x reward-to-risk target instead of 2x.

complexity.reason: same composition as V24-24 with a different reward multiple

candidates.name: PullbackNotAfterClimaxFilter
candidates.quote: Buying a high 1 pullback in a strong bull spike in a bull trend, but not after a strong buy climax.
candidates.description: Blocks a one-leg pullback entry (V24-04) when the most recent trend bar was a climax bar (V24-20); the high 1 (low 1) is only taken while the spike has not yet exhausted itself.

complexity.reason: a small backward-looking check on the climax-bar primitive

candidates.name: SpikeEntryDuringBreakout
candidates.quote: Buying a bull spike in a strong bull breakout at the market or on a limit order at or below the low of the prior bar (entering in spikes requires a wider stop and the spike happens quickly).
candidates.description: During a strong multi-bar bull trend-bar spike, enter at the market on the close of any spike bar, or on a limit order at/below the prior bar's low, rather than waiting for a pullback. Mirrored for bear spikes.
candidates.pseudocode: consecutiveTrendBars(bull) >= 2 && TrendBarBody(bull) // entry at close[0], or resting limit at low[1]-limitOffsetTicks*tickSize
candidates.book_order_type: market on the bar's close, or a resting limit order at/below the prior bar's low

complexity.reason: a short consecutive-trend-bar counter

candidates.name: WeakSignalBarLimitEntry
candidates.quote: Buying at or below a low 1 or 2 weak signal bar on a limit order in a possible new bull trend after a strong reversal up or at the bottom of a trading range.
candidates.description: Rather than waiting for a stop entry above/below a weak pullback signal bar, place a resting limit order at or below (above) that bar's low (high) when the broader context (fresh strong reversal, or range extreme) favors the trade.
candidates.pseudocode: (PullbackEntryOneLeg || PullbackEntryTwoLeg) && signalBarIsWeak(tailFraction) // resting limit at low[0]-limitOffsetTicks*tickSize
candidates.book_order_type: resting limit order at/below (at/above) the weak signal bar's low (high)

complexity.reason: reuses the pullback primitives plus a weak-bar (large tail) test

candidates.name: QuietFlagLimitEntryAtMA
candidates.quote: Buying at or below the prior bar on a limit order in a quiet bull flag at the moving average.
candidates.description: In an established trend, when price is consolidating quietly (small overlapping bars, low range) at the moving average, rest a limit order at or below the prior bar's low (above the prior bar's high for shorts) rather than waiting for a stop entry.
candidates.book_order_type: resting limit order at/below the prior bar's low

complexity.reason: an EMA-distance test plus a below-average-range 'quiet' test

candidates.name: AnticipatedBreakoutPullbackLimitEntry
candidates.quote: Buying below a bull bar that breaks above a bull flag, anticipating a breakout pullback.
candidates.description: As soon as a bull (bear) bar closes breaking out above (below) a flag/range, immediately rest a limit order below (above) that breakout bar rather than waiting for the pullback bar to actually form, anticipating BreakoutPullbackEntry (V24-10).
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] > highest(high,flagLookback,1) && TrendBarBody(bull) // resting limit at low[0]-limitOffsetTicks*tickSize placed immediately on this bar's close
candidates.book_order_type: resting limit order placed at the breakout bar's close, below its low

complexity.reason: a breakout-bar test identical to V24-10's trigger, but the order is placed one bar earlier

candidates.name: BreakoutTestAddOn
candidates.quote: When trying for a swing in a bull trend, buying or buying more on a breakout test, which is an attempt to run breakeven stops from an earlier long entry.
candidates.description: While holding (or after) a long swing entry, if price pulls back to retest the entry price area (running likely breakeven stops) and then shows a bull signal bar, add to or re-enter the long.

complexity.reason: uses position-history state (entry price) plus a signal-bar test

candidates.name: FixedTickPullbackEntry
candidates.quote: Buying a pullback in a strong bull trend at a fixed number of ticks down equal to or slightly less than the average prior pullbacks.
candidates.description: In a strong trend, rest a limit order a fixed number of ticks away from the market (set to the average size of the trend's prior pullbacks so far) rather than waiting for a specific pattern.
candidates.book_order_type: resting limit order at a fixed tick offset from the current swing extreme

complexity.reason: requires tracking and averaging the depth of prior pullbacks during the current trend

candidates.name: FailedAlwaysInFlipFade
candidates.quote: When a bear trend is about to break into a bull trend and needs one more bull trend bar to confirm the always-in reversal, and the breakout does not look strong, sell the close of the bull breakout bar, expecting the follow-through bar not to confirm the always-in flip and the bear trend to resume.
candidates.description: When price closes what would be a confirming breakout bar for an always-in flip, but that bar is weak (small body / large tail), fade it immediately at its close, betting the flip fails and the prior trend resumes.
candidates.book_order_type: market order at the close of the weak breakout bar

complexity.reason: depends entirely on the always-in read (V24-12), which itself is a design decision

candidates.name: PostClimaxReentryDelay
candidates.quote: After a final flag, traders usually wait for at least a 10-bar, two-legged pullback to the moving average before buying again.
candidates.description: After a final-flag or climax exhaustion signal, suppress with-trend re-entries until at least N bars have passed and the pullback has shown two legs to the moving average.

complexity.reason: a bar-count-since-event gate combined with the leg-count primitive

candidates.name: InitialStopBeyondSignalBar
candidates.quote: Always have a protective stop in the market... If a trader bought above bar 5, his initial stop was below bar 5.
candidates.description: The initial protective stop is placed one tick beyond the signal bar's extreme in the direction opposite the trade.

complexity.reason: a fixed offset from one identified bar

candidates.name: TightenStopToEntryBarOnConfirmation
candidates.quote: Once the market traded above the strong bar 7 two-bar reversal, he would tighten his stop to one tick below the bar 7 low.
candidates.description: Once the bar immediately following entry (or a subsequent confirming bar) closes as a trend bar in the trade's direction, move the protective stop to one tick beyond that bar's extreme, tightening the initial risk.
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.BarsSinceEntry()>=1 && TrendBarBody(direction)[0] && newStop = low[0]-stopOffsetTicks*tickSize; if newStop > currentStop then currentStop = newStop

complexity.reason: cross-bar state tracking the current stop level and only ratcheting it tighter

candidates.name: BreakevenStopAtProfitThreshold
candidates.quote: Typically, traders should not move their stops to breakeven on a trade like this until there has been about 60 to 80 cents of open profit.
candidates.description: Move the protective stop to breakeven (or a small amount worse) once open position profit reaches a minimum tick threshold.

complexity.reason: a direct read of open position profit against a fixed threshold

candidates.name: BreakevenStopAtHalfTarget
candidates.quote: Some traders move their protective stop to breakeven once the trade reaches about halfway to their profit target.
candidates.description: Move the protective stop to breakeven once open profit reaches half of the originally planned profit target distance.

complexity.reason: compares current open profit to a precomputed fraction of the planned target

candidates.name: ScaleOutHalfAtRiskEqualsReward
candidates.quote: On bar 6, traders would have been able to exit half of their shares with $1.00 profit... At this point, they would have moved their protective stop to breakeven.
candidates.description: Take partial profit (half the position) once open profit equals the amount originally risked, then move the stop on the remainder to breakeven and trail it.

complexity.reason: needs the originally-planned risk distance carried as position state, plus partial-exit bookkeeping

candidates.name: TrailStopBeyondPriorSwing
candidates.quote: They should trail this protective stop beyond swing lows on the 5 minute chart, and take a little more off at two dollars' profit.
candidates.description: Once swinging the remainder of a winning position, trail the protective stop to just beyond the most recent confirmed swing low (high for shorts).

complexity.reason: requires ongoing swing-pivot detection to identify each new confirmed swing low

candidates.name: WiderStopForSpikeEntry
candidates.quote: If they used a wide stop, they would have to reduce their position size... entering in spikes requires a wider stop and the spike happens quickly.
candidates.description: When entering during a strong multi-bar spike (V24-27) rather than on a pullback, size the protective stop as a multiple of the normal signal-bar stop distance (and correspondingly reduce position size).

complexity.reason: a fixed multiplier applied to an existing stop-distance calculation

candidates.name: SwingRewardAtLeastTwiceRisk
candidates.quote: When starting out, focus on trades where the reward is at least twice as large as the risk.
candidates.description: For swing-classified trades, set the profit target at least two times the planned protective-stop distance.

complexity.reason: a comparison of two known price distances

candidates.name: AvoidCountertrendScalpInWeakChannel
candidates.quote: Countertrend scalps are most tempting in weak channels, where the with-trend setups just don't look strong enough... An impatient trader who buys above the bull reversal bar on a stop will consistently lose money.
candidates.description: Block a counter-trend reversal-bar entry (e.g. a bull reversal bar in an established bear channel) that fades a new trend extreme, since these setups have a demonstrated negative trader's equation.

complexity.reason: depends on the always-in read plus a qualitative 'weak channel' judgment Brooks never fully formalizes

candidates.name: AvoidStopEntryInTightTradingRange
candidates.quote: If the market enters a tight trading range, wait for the breakout, because tight trading ranges trump everything... Using stop entries in a tight trading range is a losing strategy.
candidates.description: Block all stop entries while the recent N-bar range is unusually tight (small relative to the recent average range), regardless of any pattern that would otherwise trigger.

complexity.reason: a window range compared against an average-range baseline

candidates.name: MajorityBarsOnMASideFilter
candidates.quote: They should look to buy only when the market is mostly above the moving average and sell when most of the recent bars are below the moving average.
candidates.description: Only allow long entries when a clear majority of the last N bars have closed above the 20-bar EMA (mirrored: shorts only when a majority closed below).
candidates.pseudocode: countBarsAbove = countBars(close[i] > ema[i], lookback); countBarsAbove >= majorityFraction*lookback

complexity.reason: a window loop counting bars against an EMA compared to a fraction threshold

candidates.name: ConsecutiveClimaxBarsExpectCorrection
candidates.quote: Consecutive buy climaxes are usually followed by at least a two-legged correction.
candidates.description: When two or more climax bars (V24-20) occur within a short span in the same direction, treat the next opposite-direction signal bar as higher-confidence, expecting at least a two-legged correction.
candidates.pseudocode: climaxCountRecent(direction,shortLookback) >= 2 => boost confidence of the next TrendBarBody(opposite) signal

complexity.reason: a short-window count of the climax-bar primitive

candidates.name: ExtendedOneSidedRangeMoveFavorsFade
candidates.quote: In general, when the market is in a trading range and it is up for five to 10 bars, traders should only look for shorts.
candidates.description: While price is judged to be inside a trading range, if the current leg has moved in one direction for at least N consecutive bars without a real pullback, only allow fade entries against that leg (blocking with-leg entries).

complexity.reason: depends on a 'the market is in a trading range' read, which is itself a design decision, plus a consecutive-bar-in-direction counter

candidates.name: LimitOrderOnlyWithAlwaysInDirection
candidates.quote: Traders should only use limit orders to trade in the direction of the trend... he should only [buy on a limit] if the market is always-in long.
candidates.description: Block any limit-order (as opposed to stop) entry unless it is in the same direction as the current always-in read.

complexity.reason: depends entirely on the always-in primitive

candidates.name: TradingRangeVsTrendEntryBias
candidates.quote: When the market is clearly bullish, buying near the high and exiting higher is an effective strategy... When it is in a trading range, buying near the high is usually a mistake, and traders should instead try to buy near the low.
candidates.description: Switches entry bias by market regime: in a trend, buy strength (near recent highs) and sell weakness (near recent lows); in a trading range, buy near the range low and sell near the range high (invert the bias).

complexity.reason: requires a trend-vs-trading-range classifier, one of the qualitative design decisions Brooks leaves undefined

rejected.quote: Trade only a small position size. If you think that you can trade 300 shares, you should trade only 100 shares so that you are in ‘I don’t care’ mode.
rejected.reason: account-level position-sizing/psychology advice, not a bar-level OHLCV condition

rejected.quote: They actually have to win on about 80 percent of their tiny scalps to make a living at it... The reality is that they will never become that good.
rejected.reason: pure discretionary/statistical commentary about trader skill, no bar-level test

rejected.quote: Look for simple strategies. If something is not clear, wait.
rejected.reason: pure discretion with no bar-level test ('trade what makes sense')

rejected.quote: If the market is moving too fast for a trader to consider the math of the current setup, he should not take the trade.
rejected.reason: depends on the trader's own processing speed, not any market data the engine has

rejected.quote: Although the forex market is essentially a 24-hour market and has no real open, it otherwise behaves like stocks and futures and should be traded in the same way.
rejected.reason: general market-structure commentary, not a testable condition

rejected.quote: You determine the probability, which can never be known with precision... assume that there is a 50 percent chance... If you are confident about the trade, assume that the odds are 60-40.
rejected.reason: subjective probability assessment based on the trader's confidence, not derivable from OHLCV

rejected.quote: Print out weeks of charts of the time frame and market they plan to trade and see if their setups appear to be valid.
rejected.reason: a study/practice instruction to the trader, not a market condition

rejected.quote: If you trade 25 Emini contracts and net just two points a day, you will make $500,000 a year.
rejected.reason: an account-sizing/earnings illustration, not a trading condition

rejected.quote: I saw a video on YouTube where the trader carefully explained that he always traded a second Emini contract, scalping it at a one tick profit...
rejected.reason: an anecdote about another trader's account setup, not a chart-derivable rule

rejected.quote: Another common mistake is to look at 1 minute charts or other smaller time frame charts, like tick and volume charts...
rejected.reason: a timeframe-selection preference/discretionary commentary, not itself a bar-level entry/exit condition

rejected.quote: An obvious example is the incredible bull market that took place when the Republicans took control of Congress in 1994... Was this bear trend and panic sell-off caused by the subprime mess, or was it the direct result of the country realizing that Barack Obama was going to win the White House?
rejected.reason: political/fundamental commentary, data the engine cannot have

rejected.quote: Many traders will use a limit order that is one tick less than usual, knowing that the market often hits the obvious target price, but reverses instead of filling the profit-taking limit orders.

chapter_summary: Chapter 24 is the trilogy's capstone: a discursive essay on trader's-equation math and discipline, a large bulleted catalog of 'best trade' setups (opening reversals, major trend reversals, stairs patterns, measured-move exhaustion, high/low 1 and 2 pullbacks, wedge and breakout pullbacks, second entries at range extremes, and several limit-order variants), followed by 24 worked chart examples (Figures 24.1-24.24) that narrate specific numbered bars on charts not included in this text extract. Almost every pattern named (high 1/2, low 1/2, two-bar reversal, double top/bottom, wedge, final flag, breakout pullback, moving-average gap bar, always-in, trend-line break, measured move, expanding triangle, climax, micro channel) is a primitive this chapter reuses rather than introduces, so the primitives defined here (V24-01..V24-23) are expected to be near-duplicates of primitives defined in earlier chapters of all three books; the dedup pass should treat this file as confirmation/parameter-refinement of those, not a new source of unique patterns. The genuinely new material is concentrated in explicit trade-management numbers (breakeven timing, scale-out-half-at-risk, wider stops for spike entries, post-climax reentry delay) and a handful of context filters (avoid countertrend scalps in weak channels, avoid stop entries in tight ranges, majority-of-bars-vs-MA filter, extended one-sided range move favors a fade) that were stated only in narrative prose elsewhere in the book.
